6 Best Headless CMS Platforms for Developer Teams (2026)

The best headless CMS platforms in 2026 are Sanity for real-time collaborative editing, Contentful for large enterprise teams, Strapi for open-source self-hosting, Storyblok for visual editing, Hygraph for GraphQL content federation, and Directus for turning an existing SQL database into a CMS.

A headless CMS decision made on the marketing page and a headless CMS decision made after reading the API docs usually land on different vendors. The pitch pages all promise flexible content modeling and a fast API; the real differences show up in how content is structured (documents vs. components vs. an existing SQL schema), how collaborative editing actually feels, and what the bill looks like once you're past the free tier. This guide compares 6 real headless CMS platforms on verified G2 reviews, published pricing, and what each one is actually built for.
Last checked: October 2026 (pricing and G2 ratings re-verified).
Disclosure: every G2 rating and review count below was re-checked on October 21, 2026, and every dollar figure was cross-checked against each vendor's own pricing page the same day.
How we compared these platforms

Four criteria: (1) Verified reputation: real G2 reviews, not a vendor's own case-study page. (2) Pricing transparency: a published rate card, not "contact us" as the only answer past a free tier. (3) Content model: does the platform model content as flexible documents, visual components, or does it sit directly on top of a database you already have? (4) Who it's actually built for: a marketing team that needs a visual editor, or a developer team that wants a schema and an API and nothing else.

1. Sanity, best for real-time collaborative editing and the largest review base

Sanity structures content as flexible, portable-text documents editable in real time inside its Studio editor, an open-source React application you can customize down to individual field types. Its G2 profile shows 926 verified reviews at 4.7/5, the largest review count of any platform on this list by a wide margin.
Best for: developer teams that want a highly customizable, code-configurable editor and real-time multiplayer editing, and that are comfortable running or hosting Sanity Studio themselves.
Pricing: Free tier includes up to 20 seats, 2 datasets, 10,000 documents; Growth $15/seat/month (up to 50 seats), 25,000 documents; Enterprise custom.

Pros: by far the largest verified review base on this list; real-time collaborative editing (multiple people editing the same document simultaneously) is a first-class feature, not bolted on; Studio is open-source and fully customizable at the code level.

Cons: the customization that makes Sanity powerful for developers (configuring Studio in code) is also the thing a non-technical content team can't do without developer help; per-seat pricing on the Growth tier scales cost with team size in a way flat-rate competitors don't.
2. Contentful, best for the largest enterprise ecosystem

Contentful is one of the earliest and most widely adopted headless CMS platforms, with a large partner and integrations ecosystem and a content model built around structured "content types" and reference fields. Salesforce completed its acquisition of Contentful on September 1, 2026, according to Salesforce's newsroom. Its G2 profile shows 399 verified reviews at 4.3/5, the lowest rating on this list, though still solidly positive.
Best for: large organizations that want an established, widely integrated platform with a big partner network for implementation help, and that need multi-space, multi-brand governance.

Pricing: Free tier includes 10 users, 100K API calls/month; Lite $300/month on Contentful's own pricing page (20 users, 1M API calls/month; the page has also shown €300/month to euro-region visitors); Enterprise custom with unlimited API calls and dedicated support.

Pros: largest and most established partner/integrations ecosystem on this list, useful for teams that want implementation help rather than building everything in-house; generous free-tier API call allowance (100K/month) for early-stage projects; extensive governance and compliance features (SSO, SCIM, ISO 27001) at the Enterprise tier.

Cons: lowest G2 rating on this list, and Contentful's pricing page renders by billing region (we have seen Lite at both $300/month and €300/month), so get the exact figure for your own account's currency before comparing costs directly against the other platforms here; the jump from the free tier to Lite is a larger step than several competitors' entry paid tiers.
3. Strapi, best for open-source, self-hosted deployment with no vendor lock-in

Strapi is a fully open-source (MIT-licensed) headless CMS you self-host, with unlimited entries and API calls at zero software cost on the Community tier, plus a hosted Cloud option and paid tiers for teams that want managed infrastructure and support instead. Its G2 profile shows 206 verified reviews at 4.5/5.
Best for: teams that want full control over hosting and data, and that specifically want to avoid recurring per-seat SaaS pricing for a self-managed deployment.
Pricing: Community tier is free forever (self-hosted, unlimited entries and API calls); Growth $45/month (3 seats included, $15/month per additional seat); Enterprise custom.

Pros: genuinely free and open-source at the core, not a crippled trial tier; unlimited entries and API calls even on the free Community tier since you're hosting it yourself; a REST API out of the box, with GraphQL added through Strapi's official GraphQL plugin.
Cons: self-hosting means you own infrastructure, upgrades, and uptime unless you pay for the Cloud or Growth tier; smaller review base than Sanity, Storyblok, or Hygraph.
4. Storyblok, best for visual, component-based editing that marketers and developers both use

Storyblok structures content as nestable, reusable components edited through a visual page-builder interface, so a marketer can rearrange a page's sections without touching code while developers define what each component can contain. Its G2 profile shows 598 verified reviews at 4.5/5.
Best for: teams where marketing or content staff need to build and edit pages visually, not just fill in text fields, while developers still control the underlying component logic.
Pricing: Free Starter tier includes 1 space, 1 seat, 100GB traffic/month; Growth $99/month (5 seats, 400GB traffic); Growth Plus $349/month (15 seats, 1TB traffic); Premium and Elite custom.

Pros: visual component editor is a genuine differentiator for non-technical content teams, not just a form-based field editor; every space includes a 45-day free trial of the Growth Plus tier before you commit to a plan; AI credits are bundled into every tier, including the free one.

Cons: single-space limit even on the Growth and Growth Plus tiers means multi-brand or multi-site setups likely need Premium/Elite custom pricing; traffic-based limits (GB/month) are a different cost axis than the API-call-based limits most competitors here use, making direct cost comparison less straightforward.
5. Hygraph, best for GraphQL-native, federated multi-source content

Hygraph (formerly GraphCMS) is built GraphQL-first and specifically supports federating content from more than one source, including external systems, into a single unified API, rather than assuming all content lives inside the CMS itself. Its G2 profile shows 733 verified reviews at 4.4/5, the second-largest review base on this list.
Best for: teams with content or product data spread across multiple systems that want one GraphQL API surface over all of it, not just their own CMS content.

Pricing: Hobby tier is free forever (3 seats, 1,000 entries, 500,000 API calls/month); Growth from $199/month (10 seats, 10,000 entries, 1,000,000 API calls/month, one remote source connection); Enterprise custom.

Pros: second-largest verified review base on this list; content federation (unifying multiple content sources behind one API) is a genuine, distinctive capability most competitors here don't offer; GraphQL-first design fits naturally into a modern frontend stack that already queries via GraphQL elsewhere.
Cons: the $199/month Growth tier costs more than Strapi's or Storyblok's entry paid tiers; the free Hobby tier's 1,000-entry cap is restrictive for anything beyond a small project.
6. Directus, best for turning an existing database into a CMS and API instantly

Directus takes a fundamentally different approach from the rest of this list: instead of defining its own content model, it wraps an existing SQL database (Postgres, MySQL, SQL Server, and others) and instantly exposes a REST and GraphQL API plus an admin UI over your actual schema, no matter how it was originally designed. Its G2 profile shows 53 verified reviews at 4.8/5, the highest rating of any platform on this list.
Best for: teams that already have a database (or are building one) and want a CMS-style admin UI and API layered on top of it, rather than migrating content into a new, CMS-specific data model.

Pricing: Core tier is free (self-hosted, 3 user seats, 25 collections, includes an AI Assistant); Team $499/month annual commitment or $599/month rolling monthly (10 SSO seats, 50 collections, self-hosted); Directus Cloud hosting is a $99/month add-on on Core and Team; Enterprise custom. A separate Open Innovation Grant offers full features free (self-hosted) or at $99/month (cloud) to qualifying organizations under $5M revenue and 50 employees.

Pros: highest G2 rating on this list; works directly on top of a database you already have instead of requiring content migration into a new model; the Open Innovation Grant is a real, published discount path for small organizations, not a vague "contact us for a discount."

Cons: smallest review base on this list (53), though the rating itself is the strongest; the Team tier's $499-599/month price is the highest paid entry point of any platform here, though the free self-hosted Core tier has no seat-based cost at all.

When a headless CMS platform is the wrong call

Every platform above assumes someone on your team can define a content model, wire up the frontend to the API, and maintain that integration as requirements change. If the actual need is a fully custom application with logic well beyond content display, not a content-managed site or app, a headless CMS can end up as an awkward middle layer rather than a fit. ManasFlow's SaaS MVP development service builds custom web applications directly, choosing a CMS layer only where content structure genuinely calls for one rather than defaulting to it. If the gap is engineering capacity to implement and maintain one of the platforms above, AI engineer placement covers hiring direct instead.
Red flags when evaluating a headless CMS
A free tier with no clear published path to what the next tier actually costs at real scale, only "contact us."
A vendor demo that only shows content creation, not what happens when your frontend needs a field type or relationship the platform doesn't natively support.
No mention of what content migration out of the platform looks like if you need to leave. Vendor lock-in risk is real and worth asking about directly, not assuming it away.

Pricing based on a metric (seats, API calls, traffic, entries) that doesn't match how your team or application will actually scale. Confirm which axis matters for your specific use case before comparing sticker prices across platforms.
No answer for how the platform handles localization or multi-language content if that's a real requirement, since retrofitting it later is expensive on some platforms and native on others.
FAQ
What is a headless CMS?

A headless CMS manages content through an API without dictating how or where that content is displayed, unlike a traditional CMS (like WordPress) that couples content management to a specific front-end templating system. A developer builds the actual website or app separately and pulls content from the CMS's API.
How much does a headless CMS cost?

Every platform on this list offers a free tier for small projects or evaluation. Paid tiers for real production use typically start between $45 and $199/month (Strapi, Storyblok, Hygraph), with Contentful's Lite tier at $300/month (€300 in euro regions) and Directus's Team tier at $499/month billed annually. Self-hosted open-source options (Strapi, Directus) can run at zero software cost if you're willing to manage your own infrastructure.
Should I choose a self-hosted or SaaS headless CMS?

A self-hosted option (Strapi, Directus's free Core tier) gives you full control over data and infrastructure at the cost of managing hosting, upgrades, and uptime yourself. A SaaS platform (Sanity, Contentful, Storyblok, Hygraph, or Directus with its $99/month cloud hosting add-on) handles infrastructure for you at a recurring cost that typically scales with seats, API calls, or traffic.
What's the difference between a document-based, component-based, and database-first headless CMS?

A document-based CMS (Sanity, Contentful) models content as structured records with defined fields and relationships. A component-based CMS (Storyblok) models content as nestable, reusable visual building blocks a non-technical editor can arrange. A database-first tool (Directus) skips defining a new content model entirely and instead exposes an API and admin UI directly over a SQL database you already have or are building.
What are the best headless CMS solutions for developer teams?

Sanity, Strapi and Directus fit developer teams best. Sanity gives you an editor configured in code, Strapi gives you an open-source CMS you host yourself, and Directus puts an API and admin UI on a SQL database you already run. Pick Storyblok instead if marketers need to rearrange pages visually.
Which headless CMS has the strongest API for custom development?

For custom development, Hygraph and Directus give you the most API surface. Hygraph is GraphQL-first and can federate content from other systems into one API; Directus generates REST and GraphQL APIs over a SQL database you already run. Sanity queries content with GROQ and can also deploy a GraphQL API, Contentful has REST delivery and GraphQL content APIs, Storyblok has a REST delivery API plus a read-only GraphQL API, and Strapi ships REST with GraphQL as an official plugin.
What GraphQL support do the leading headless CMS platforms have?

Hygraph is built on GraphQL. Directus and Contentful offer GraphQL next to REST. Sanity can deploy a GraphQL API alongside its native GROQ queries. Storyblok's GraphQL API is read-only and region-specific, so it is for delivery, not writes. Strapi adds GraphQL with @strapi/plugin-graphql. Check the tier you plan to buy, since rate limits and plan rules differ.
Which headless CMS is best for developers and marketers working together?

Storyblok, because marketers can rearrange pages in its visual component editor while developers define what each component can hold. Sanity is the other strong pick: several people can edit the same document in real time, but the editor itself is configured in code, so marketers depend on developers for changes to it.
Can one headless CMS serve several websites from the same content library?

Yes. A headless CMS is not tied to one front end, so several sites and apps can read the same content through the API. What to compare is how each platform separates them: locales per site, roles and permissions per site or brand, preview per front end, and whether references can cross spaces or datasets. On Storyblok, the Growth tiers are limited to one space, so multi-site setups often land on Premium or Elite.
How do you migrate from Contentful or Sanity to another headless CMS?

Export the content through the vendor's own tooling (contentful space export in the Contentful CLI, sanity dataset export in the Sanity CLI), map each content type to the new platform's model, then import with the target's API and re-point the front end. Rich text is usually the slow part, because each platform stores it differently (Contentful rich text JSON, Sanity Portable Text).
Is Contentful still an independent company?
No. Salesforce completed its acquisition of Contentful on September 1, 2026. The Free, Lite and Enterprise plans were still listed on Contentful's pricing page when we checked on October 21, 2026.
Can a headless CMS handle multi-language content?

Most platforms on this list support localization natively, though the depth varies: Contentful and Sanity support multiple locales even on lower tiers, Storyblok scales locale count with plan tier, and Hygraph's entry-level tier caps locale-dependent features more tightly. Confirm the specific locale limits on your target tier before assuming a platform's marketing page claim applies at your price point.
Do I need a developer to set up a headless CMS?

Generally yes, at least for initial setup. Every platform on this list requires a developer to define the content model (or, for Directus, to already have a database) and to build the frontend that consumes the API. Ongoing content editing after setup can be handled by non-technical staff on all six platforms, though Storyblok's visual editor goes furthest in letting a non-developer restructure a page's layout, not just fill in fields.
The platform is not the hard part

Every CMS on this list can technically store and serve the content you have in mind. The actual constraint is almost always the integration work: wiring the frontend to the API correctly, modeling content in a way that survives real editorial use, and maintaining that integration as requirements change, not which vendor's demo looked the cleanest.
